experiences/francis-stigmata-la-verna/ti: Francis of Assisi receives the stigmata at La Verna
experiences/francis-stigmata-la-verna/ac: Paraphrase of Thomas of Celano (First Life, 1229) and Bonaventure (Major Legend 13): around the feast of the Exaltation of the Cross (14 September) 1224, while fasting on Mount La Verna, Francis sees a seraph with six wings, fixed to a cross. As the vision fades, marks like nails appear in his hands and feet and a wound in his side. Brother Elias' letter announcing Francis' death (1226) is the earliest text to mention the marks.
experiences/francis-stigmata-la-verna/co: Contemporaries took the stigmata as a seal showing Francis as an 'alter Christus'. Some Dominicans and secular clergy questioned the claim; Pope Gregory IX issued bulls (1237) defending it. It is generally considered the first reported case of stigmata.
experiences/francis-stigmata-la-verna/as: The stigmata are commemorated in a feast (17 September) and widely accepted as a supernatural grace, though the Church does not require belief in them.
Orthodox tradition has no stigmatics and is reserved about the phenomenon, seeing a Western emphasis on imitating Christ's physical suffering that differs from Eastern stress on transfiguration.
Usually doubtful or agnostic; Francis is widely admired for poverty and peacemaking, but the stigmata are often attributed to pious embellishment.

Elias' early letter and multiple witnesses make the claim of visible marks well attested as a belief; explanations range from genuine wounds of unknown cause to self-inflicted or psychosomatic wounds or later elaboration (André Vauchez discusses the sources).
experiences/francis-stigmata-la-verna/de: Authenticity and possible natural causes of stigmata.
Why stigmata appear almost exclusively in Latin Catholicism after 1224.
experiences/francis-stigmata-la-verna/st:
Francis of Assisi (born Giovanni di Pietro di Bernardone around 1181-1182) was the son of a wealthy cloth merchant in Umbria. After a youth of ambition and a spell as a prisoner of war, he underwent a gradual conversion around 1205-1206: he embraced lepers, rebuilt ruined churches and renounced his inheritance before the bishop of Assisi. Followers gathered around his life of radical poverty, preaching and penance, and Pope Innocent III gave verbal approval to their way of life around 1209-1210. By the 1220s the Order of Friars Minor numbered thousands, and Francis, worn out by illness and troubled by the order's institutional growth, had handed over its day-to-day government.

La Verna is a wooded mountain in the Casentino region of Tuscany. In 1213 Count Orlando of Chiusi gave it to Francis as a place of retreat. In the late summer of 1224 Francis went there with a few close companions, among them Brother Leo, to keep a forty-day fast in honour of St Michael the Archangel, from the feast of the Assumption (15 August) to Michaelmas (29 September).

According to Thomas of Celano's First Life of Francis, written in 1228-1229, about two years before his death Francis saw in a vision a man like a seraph with six wings, standing above him with hands outstretched and feet joined, fixed to a cross. Two wings were raised above his head, two spread for flight and two covered his body. Francis was filled with joy at the seraph's gracious look and with sorrow at the crucifixion, and while he was wondering what it meant, the marks of nails began to appear in his hands and feet, and a wound in his right side, which often bled. Later accounts, especially Bonaventure's Major Legend (1260-1263), place the vision around the feast of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross, 14 September 1224, and identify the seraph as Christ himself.

Francis tried to conceal the wounds, keeping his hands covered and wearing shoes, and only a few companions saw them during his life. On La Verna he wrote on a small piece of parchment the Praises of God and a blessing for Brother Leo; this 'chartula', one of only two autographs of Francis that survive, is preserved in Assisi, and Leo's notes on it link its writing to the vision of the seraph and the imprinting of the stigmata. Francis came down from the mountain and, though increasingly ill and nearly blind, composed the Canticle of Brother Sun in 1225.

Francis died at the Portiuncula near Assisi on the evening of 3 October 1226. Brother Elias of Cortona, the order's vicar, immediately sent a circular letter announcing that Francis had borne the marks of Christ's passion, describing them as nails formed of his flesh. Witnesses who examined the body, according to Celano and other early sources, described black nail-like formations in the hands and feet and a red wound in the side. Francis was canonised by Pope Gregory IX on 16 July 1228, less than two years after his death.

The stigmata were contested from the start. Some clergy, including a bishop in Moravia and members of rival orders, doubted or denied them, and Gregory IX issued bulls in 1237 defending their authenticity. Bonaventure's Legend, adopted by the Franciscan order in 1266 as its official life, made the stigmata the climax of Francis' identification with Christ.

Modern historians have weighed several possibilities: genuine supernatural marks, as Catholic tradition holds; self-inflicted wounds, conscious or unconscious; a psychosomatic phenomenon; or a later embellishment of signs of illness, such as the leprosy he may have contracted. Some scholars have also noted that Francis' early followers had strong reasons to present him as an alter Christus. The documentary evidence, including Elias' letter and Leo's note, shows at least that the claim was made within days of his death by people who knew him.

experiences/francis-stigmata-la-verna/si: Francis' stigmata are the first widely reported case of the phenomenon in Christian history and set a pattern for hundreds of later stigmatics, from Catherine of Siena to Padre Pio. They became central to Franciscan identity and to late medieval devotion to Christ's suffering humanity, influencing art (Giotto's frescoes in Assisi among many others) and piety. Protestant reformers were sceptical of such marvels, and modern historians debate whether the stigmata were miraculous, psychosomatic, self-inflicted or partly hagiographic constructions. The episode remains a key case in the study of religious experience, the body and sanctity.
experiences/catherine-of-siena-mystical/: Catherine of Siena: mystical espousal and invisible stigmata
Pisa

Paraphrase of Raymond of Capua's Legenda Maior: Catherine experienced a 'mystical marriage' to Christ (c. 1368) and, at Pisa on 1 April 1375, after communion, rays from the crucified Christ pierced her hands, feet and side; at her prayer the wounds remained invisible, causing pain but no marks. Her disciples recorded her dictating The Dialogue while in ecstasy (1377-78).

Her ecstatic authority lent weight to her letters urging Pope Gregory XI to return from Avignon to Rome (1376-77). Franciscans contested Dominican claims of her stigmata; Pope Sixtus IV (a Franciscan) at one point forbade depicting them.
Catholic
Saint, Doctor of the Church (1970) and co-patron of Europe; her mystical experiences are treated as authentic graces, though the invisible-stigmata claim is not a matter of faith.
Protestant
Admired for courageous church reform and social service; extreme fasting and ecstatic claims are often viewed critically.
Historian
Caroline Walker Bynum interprets her extreme fasting and eucharistic piety as a form of female religious agency; Raymond's Life is hagiography written to support canonisation.
Psychology of religion
Her refusal of food has been debated as 'holy anorexia' (Rudolph Bell), a diagnosis others reject as anachronistic.
Female mystics, fasting and authority.
Rivalry between religious orders over stigmata claims.

Fourteenth-century Italy was shaken by plague, by wars between city-states and by the absence of the popes, who had lived at Avignon since 1309. Catherine Benincasa was born in Siena in 1347, the year before the Black Death reached the city, one of the youngest of a very large family; her father Jacopo was a wool dyer. According to her confessor and biographer Raymond of Capua, she saw a vision of Christ above the church of San Domenico when she was about six and soon after vowed virginity. She resisted her family's plans for her marriage, cut off her hair and was eventually allowed to join the Mantellate, a group of mostly widowed Dominican tertiaries who lived at home, around 1363-1364.

For about three years she lived in near seclusion in a small room in her family's house, praying, fasting and sleeping little. Around 1367-1368 she experienced what Raymond describes as a mystical marriage to Christ, who gave her a ring visible only to herself. Soon after, she reported, Christ told her to go out and serve others. She began nursing the sick and plague victims, caring for prisoners and the poor, and gathered a circle of followers, men and women, clerics and lay people, who called her 'mamma'. Her extreme fasting became notorious: Raymond reports that for long periods she could take little or nothing but the Eucharist, and critics accused her of hypocrisy or pride.

On 1 April 1375, while visiting Pisa, Catherine received communion in the little church of Santa Cristina. According to Raymond, who was present and wrote the account a decade or more later, she fell into ecstasy and afterwards told him that she had seen the crucified Lord coming toward her in great light, and that rays of blood-red light came from the five wounds toward her hands, feet and heart. She asked that the marks not be visible, and the rays, she said, turned to pure light before reaching her. She reported feeling the pain of the wounds for the rest of her life. According to Raymond, the marks became visible on her body only after her death.

Catherine's influence grew far beyond Siena. She dictated hundreds of letters (about 380 survive) to popes, rulers, mercenary captains and ordinary people. In 1376 she travelled to Avignon to plead with Pope Gregory XI to return to Rome and to make peace with Florence. Gregory did return in January 1377, though historians debate how decisive her influence was. In 1377-1378 she dictated her major work, the Dialogue, a conversation between the soul and God on discernment, providence, obedience and prayer, written partly while in ecstasy according to her disciples.

When the Great Western Schism broke out in 1378, with rival popes in Rome and Avignon, Catherine supported Urban VI and moved to Rome to work for him. Exhausted by fasting and grief at the divided Church, she died there on 29 April 1380, aged thirty-three. Raymond of Capua, later master general of the Dominicans, wrote her Legenda maior to promote her canonisation, which Pope Pius II, himself a Sienese, proclaimed in 1461.

Her stigmata were disputed, especially by Franciscans, who regarded the stigmata as a unique privilege of Francis; Pope Sixtus IV, a Franciscan, is reported to have forbidden depictions of her with visible wounds, and artists often showed rays instead. Modern historians have also discussed her fasting in light of what Rudolph Bell called 'holy anorexia' (1985), a reading others criticise as projecting a modern diagnosis onto a different religious culture. In 1970 Paul VI named her one of the first two women Doctors of the Church, together with Teresa of Ávila, and in 1999 John Paul II made her a co-patron of Europe.

Catherine of Siena showed how a laywoman without formal education could, through a reputation for mystical experience, exercise remarkable public authority in church politics, diplomacy and spiritual teaching. Her Dialogue and letters are classics of Italian literature and Catholic spirituality, and her example shaped later models of active, apostolic holiness for women. Her stigmata, and the dispute with Franciscans over them, show how claims of mystical favour were contested along institutional lines. Modern scholars debate her fasting, the role of Raymond of Capua in shaping her image and the extent of her political influence, while Catholics honour her as a Doctor of the Church and patron of Italy and Europe.
